source_read: PMC HTML (PMC6792853; J Neurosci 1998;18:8417-8422): abstract, unheaded introduction, Materials and Methods, Tables 1-3, Results (demographics, drug use, caudate, putamen), Figure 1 legend, Discussion, funding footnote.

claims.overstatement: The population wording 'scanned after days to months of abstinence' does not fit this study: by Table 2 the six methamphetamine users had last used 4 to 65 months before PET (mean about 33 months; abstract 'about 3 years'), so this source extends the finding to years of abstinence rather than days to months. Otherwise no overstatement.
claims.note: The -23% caudate and -25% putamen figures (6 vs 10) reproduce from Table 3 uncorrected binding potentials (5.8 vs 7.5 = -22.7%; 5.5 vs 7.3 = -24.7%). The authors' age-corrected values give about -19.5% and -19.3% (7.0 vs 8.7; 6.7 vs 8.3); users were 7 years older on average (37.5 vs 30.5, not significant). Editors' standardized differences (Hedges' g, uncorrected): caudate -1.08, putamen -1.37. Individual values are not shown, so overlap cannot be checked directly; the SDs imply overlap (control caudate 7.5 +/- 1.7 vs users 5.8 +/- 1.0). The authors raise neuroadaptation as an alternative to terminal loss but do not discuss pre-existing differences.

anchors.locator: Table 3; Results > Caudate nucleus and Putamen
anchors.extracted: [11C]WIN-35,428 binding potential (k3/k4). Controls (n=10) caudate 7.5 +/- 1.7, putamen 7.3 +/- 1.4; methamphetamine users (n=6) 5.8 +/- 1.0 and 5.5 +/- 0.9 (-23%, -25%); age-corrected 8.7 vs 7.0 and 8.3 vs 6.7 (about -20% and -19%). ANCOVA with age: caudate F(3,18)=4.97 (printed p=0.039), putamen F(3,18)=5.53, p=0.007; post hoc Duncan tests users < controls in both regions.

Users recruited from rehabilitation groups; usual 1/4 to 3 1/2 g/day for 3-20 years by self-report; mixed routes; all screened negative before PET; time from last use to PET 4-65 months (abstract: about 3 years on average). All had used other drugs (cannabis, LSD, benzodiazepines, cocaine, alcohol).

claims.overstatement: None. The claim is more cautious than the authors, who 'tend to favor' neurotoxicity on the basis of animal evidence and the similarity with Parkinson's disease, but the authors themselves state that a neuroadaptive process cannot be excluded.
claims.note: Supported: lower DAT; the authors concede the measure cannot separate terminal loss from neuroadaptation (and that binding potential could reflect Bmax or Kd); the users' reductions were smaller than in early PD, not putamen-predominant as in PD, and without clinical parkinsonism. Qualification: this study's reductions were present after a mean of about 3 years of abstinence (cross-sectional), which weighs against full reversibility in these six people; the recovery part of the claim rests on other sources. A post-mortem study (Wilson 1996) is described as finding normal DDC and VMAT2 in users, which the authors argue are insensitive markers.

anchors.extracted: Authors ask whether the reduction reflects neuroadaptation rather than neurotoxicity; they favour neurotoxicity because of animal evidence and the resemblance to PD, but acknowledge decreases in DAT could reflect a compensatory process without terminal degeneration, citing pharmacological manipulations that change DAT density.

Early PD (n=3): caudate -47%, putamen -68%, putamen-predominant and significantly lower than users in putamen; methamphetamine users caudate -23%, putamen -25% (similar in both regions); no clinical signs of parkinsonism in users.

Post-mortem study in chronic users (Wilson 1996a) found DAT loss but normal DDC and VMAT, concluding no neurotoxicity; authors argue these markers are insensitive to milder injury. Binding potential could change through Bmax or Kd. Summary: results raise the possibility of neurotoxicity, 'although a neuroadaptive process is also conceivable'; reductions less severe than early PD and not associated with overt neurological or psychiatric illness; longitudinal studies needed.
Reductions observed after 4-65 months since last use (mean about 3 years) in a cross-sectional comparison; no within-person follow-up.

key_findings.correction: Recomputed: caudate g 1.08 (0.00 to 2.16), putamen 1.37 (0.25 to 2.49); methcathinone 1.09 and 0.91.

Five of six methamphetamine users (not four) reported usual amounts of 1/4 to 1/2 g/day (three 1/4, two 1/4-1/2) and one reported 3 1/2 g/day (Table 2), as the card's own exposure field states. Also, the Methods say all users had used other recreational drugs and list cannabis, LSD, benzodiazepines, cocaine and alcohol; they do not say that every user had used all five.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in step 1; p for F(3,18)=4.97 is 0.011.
Two-group t-test from Table 3: t about 1.65, df 12, p about 0.13.
Age reversal found independently in step 1.
Methods describe medical and neurological examination only.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. The Discussion is more balanced than the abstract (it names neuroadaptation as an alternative and calls for longitudinal studies); the gap lies mainly in the abstract's terminal-loss and parkinsonism-risk framing.

missed: The ANCOVA is a four-group model with age as covariate that includes the Parkinson's group (mean age 53, range 45-65), so the age slope used to adjust the user-control contrast is estimated partly from older patients with a different disease; the two-group age-corrected comparison relies instead on an external 0.8%/year assumption (Materials and Methods > Data analysis; Table 3 legend).

For cl_meth_dat_lower: this study's users were scanned months to years after last use (4-65 months; mean about 3 years), not 'days to months' as the claim's population wording says; the claim's percentages (-23%, -25%) are the uncorrected values, and the age-corrected differences are about -20% and -19%.
